title: Aggregated External AI & Tech News
description: Merged headlines from configured external sources

items.title: Thousands of consumer routers hacked by Russia's military (Source: feeds.arstechnica.com)
items.content_text: End-of-life routers in homes and small offices hacked in 120 countries.

items.title: OpenClaw gives users yet another reason to be freaked out about security (Source: feeds.arstechnica.com)
items.content_text: The viral AI agentic tool let attackers silently gain admin unauthenticated access.

items.title: New Rowhammer attacks give complete control of machines running Nvidia GPUs (Source: feeds.arstechnica.com)
items.content_text: GDDRHammer, GeForge and GPUBreach hammer GPU memory in ways that hijack the CPU.

items.title: Quantum computers need vastly fewer resources than thought to break vital encryption (Source: feeds.arstechnica.com)
items.content_text: No, the sky isn't falling, but Q Day is coming, and it won't be as expensive as thought.

items.title: Google bumps up Q Day deadline to 2029, far sooner than previously thought (Source: feeds.arstechnica.com)
items.content_text: Company warns entire industry to move off RSA and EC more quickly.

items.title: Self-propagating malware poisons open source software and wipes Iran-based machines (Source: feeds.arstechnica.com)
items.content_text: Development houses: It's time to check your networks for infections.

items.title: Widely used Trivy scanner compromised in ongoing supply-chain attack (Source: feeds.arstechnica.com)
items.content_text: Admins: Sorry to say, but it's likely a rotate-your-secrets kind of weekend.

items.title: Cloud service providers ask EU regulator to reinstate VMware partner program (Source: feeds.arstechnica.com)
items.content_text: Broadcom says the group is misrepresenting market "realities."

items.title: Federal cyber experts called Microsoft's cloud a "pile of shit," approved it anyway (Source: feeds.arstechnica.com)
items.content_text: One Microsoft product was approved despite years of concerns about its security.

items.title: Researchers disclose vulnerabilities in IP KVMs from four manufacturers (Source: feeds.arstechnica.com)
items.content_text: Internet-exposed devices that give BIOS-level access? What could possibly go wrong?

items.title: Supply-chain attack using invisible code hits GitHub and other repositories (Source: feeds.arstechnica.com)
items.content_text: Unicode that's invisible to the human eye was largely abandoned-until attackers took notice.

items.title: The who, what, and why of the attack that has shut down Stryker's Windows network (Source: feeds.arstechnica.com)
items.content_text: Company says it doesn't know how long it will take to restore its Microsoft environment.

items.title: 14,000 routers are infected by malware that's highly resistant to takedowns (Source: feeds.arstechnica.com)
items.content_text: Most of the devices are made by Asus and are located in the US.

items.title: Feds take notice of iOS vulnerabilities exploited under mysterious circumstances (Source: feeds.arstechnica.com)
items.content_text: The long, strange trip of a large assembly of advanced iOS exploits.

items.title: Amazon appears to be down, with over 20,000 reported problems (Source: feeds.arstechnica.com)
items.content_text: Problems viewing products and checking out.

items.title: Trump gets data center companies to pledge to pay for power generation (Source: feeds.arstechnica.com)
items.content_text: With no enforcement and questionable economics, it may not make a difference.

items.title: Downdetector, Speedtest sold to IT service-provider Accenture in $1.2B deal (Source: feeds.arstechnica.com)
items.content_text: Accenture plans to buy Ookla, which also includes RootMetrics and Ekahau.

items.title: LLMs can unmask pseudonymous users at scale with surprising accuracy (Source: feeds.arstechnica.com)
items.content_text: Pseudonymity has never been perfect for preserving privacy. Soon it may be pointless.

items.title: Google quantum-proofs HTTPS by squeezing 15kB of data into 700-byte space (Source: feeds.arstechnica.com)
items.content_text: Merkle Tree Certificate support is already in Chrome. Soon, it will be everywhere.

items.title: New AirSnitch attack bypasses Wi-Fi encryption in homes, offices, and enterprises (Source: feeds.arstechnica.com)
items.content_text: That guest network you set up for your neighbors may not be as secure as you think.
